assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect opened a new classification of electronic phases based on band topology rather than symmetry breaking. It is the kind of conceptual surprise in condensed matter that I value, and it is closely tied to quantitative band-structure calculations and to measured transport and spectroscopy.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall proposal for graphene; Molenkamp's group made the decisive HgTe/CdTe transport observation after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction. The supplied credit omits the BHZ theorists (Zhang is deceased, Bernevig and Hughes are not listed) and the 3D topological-insulator experiments (Hasan, Kane-Moore-Fu), so the allocation is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: independent confirmations in many materials and techniques (transport, ARPES, spin-resolved spectroscopy) over nearly two decades, a stable interpretation, and a large downstream field. Recognition is timely or somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: Graphene itself has too small a spin-orbit gap for a practical quantum spin Hall state, so the original material proposal was not the realized one.
Fair credit among Kane-Mele, BHZ, Molenkamp and the 3D topological-insulator discoverers is contested and cannot be settled from the supplied names alone.
This list overlaps with the quantum anomalous Hall candidate, so the committee may prefer one framing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed correlated insulators, superconductivity and related phases in moire flat bands, creating a tunable platform for strongly correlated electrons. The discovery is original and has a clear physical statement, and I would judge it highly Nobel-worthy for condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 observation of correlated insulator and superconducting states. Bistritzer is a legitimate co-theorist, but a two-person split between theory and experiment is the cleaner configuration. The role of the first authors of the 2018 papers (a graduate student and postdoc) is a question for the committee.
assessment.maturity: Quite mature in experimental terms: many independent groups reproduced the phases within a few years. The mechanism of superconductivity and the nature of the correlated states are still debated, which makes the theory side less settled and the timing arguably slightly early.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated insulators are unresolved.
Sample-to-sample variation (twist-angle disorder) is a reproducibility concern.
Earlier moire and twisted-graphene work (e.g. Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto; Cao et al.; Kim et al.) could complicate credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Femtosecond demagnetization and all-optical magnetic switching showed that magnetization can be manipulated on timescales far shorter than spin-lattice relaxation, opening ultrafast magnetism. This is directly my field and links to ongoing synchrotron and XFEL experiments; the discovery is clear and consequential for both fundamental understanding and data storage.
assessment.attribution: Beaurepaire and colleagues reported the 1996 subpicosecond demagnetization of nickel; Kimel and Rasing demonstrated non-thermal optical control and all-optical switching. The distinction between the two discoveries suggests a compound credit, and others (e.g. Stanciu, Hohlfeld, Bigot, Radu, Stohr) contributed substantial parts, so the supplied three-person configuration is defensible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally robust and reproduced widely, but the microscopic mechanism of ultrafast demagnetization (spin-flip scattering, superdiffusive transport, direct light-spin coupling) is still disputed, so the theory does not yet explain it quantitatively. This limits maturity relative to the topological candidates.
uncertainties: The microscopic explanation of ultrafast demagnetization remains unresolved.
Boundaries between demagnetization and all-optical switching credit are unclear.
As a close specialist I may be biased toward this subfield, so I treat my own enthusiasm with some caution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum anomalous Hall effect in magnetic topological insulators produces quantized, dissipationless edge transport at zero field. It combines a first-principles materials prediction with a difficult experimental realization, which is the theory-experiment link I find most convincing.
assessment.attribution: Fang and Dai made the 2010 materials prediction (Cr or Fe doped Bi2Te3 family) building on Haldane's earlier model; Xue's group delivered the 2013 observation. Haldane's role as originator and the Yu/Zhang theory contribution are not in the supplied credit, which is a significant attribution gap if the prize touches this topic.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by several independent groups and extended to higher temperature and intrinsic magnetic topological insulators (MnBi2Te4), but the quantization temperature remains low, and metrological applications are still developing. Reasonably mature, though the field is still moving.
uncertainties: Haldane's earlier model and the 2010 Science prediction by others may need to be credited.
The relationship to a possible topological-insulator prize is unsettled; two related prizes may be unlikely in short order.
Practical quantization temperatures remain well below the gap scale.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Current-induced spin-orbit torques enable electrical switching of magnetization without an external polarizer and underlie SOT-MRAM. It is a clear, well-defined condensed-matter discovery with strong technological relevance, and its quantitative understanding connects to spin-orbit physics in interfaces that I know well.
assessment.attribution: Miron and Gambardella reported Rashba-type switching in Pt/Co/AlOx; Buhrman's group demonstrated switching by the spin Hall effect from heavy metals. The relative roles of the Rashba-Edelstein and spin Hall mechanisms, and of the earlier theoretical work (Dyakonov-Perel, Hirsch, Manchon and Zhang), complicate allocation.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced by many groups with industrial development in progress. The relative contribution of bulk spin Hall versus interfacial effects is still not fully resolved.
uncertainties: The microscopic origin (spin Hall versus interfacial Rashba) of the torques remains contested.
Credit is split between spin Hall and Rashba lines, and theorists are not in the list.
Scientific novelty may be judged less fundamental than the topological or correlated-matter candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of strongly correlated matter with ultracold atoms in optical lattices realized the Mott-superfluid transition and Hubbard physics in clean, tunable systems. It provides quantitative checks of many-body theory, which I like, and it has become a foundational platform.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and colleagues) made the theoretical proposal; Greiner and Bloch performed the 2002 Mott insulator experiment, with Esslinger's fermionic work and Cirac's theory as parallel contributions. With five credited names, choosing three requires leaving out strong contributors; the allocation is therefore delicate.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely confirmed, with quantum-gas microscopes and extension to fermions. Whether the simulators have yet solved an open problem of condensed matter (such as the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram) remains an open question.
uncertainties: Competing credit for Esslinger and Cirac, and for the Bose-Einstein condensation-era pioneers, makes a three-person set contestable.
The physics prize has already recognized ultracold-atom BEC, so a further cold-atom prize may be considered redundant.
Quantitative advantage over classical simulation of Hubbard models is not yet decisively demonstrated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of iron-based high-temperature superconductors in 2008 revealed a second family of high-Tc materials with multiband magnetism-related pairing. It is a significant materials discovery that drew heavy first-principles theory and spectroscopy attention.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's group made the original LaFeAsO(F) discovery; the subsequent rapid increase of Tc by Chen and Zhao's groups was important but derivative. A sole-laureate configuration is the most defensible reading, but it is a judgement call among the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Well replicated, but the pairing mechanism is still not understood after more than fifteen years and Tc values remain below cuprates at ambient pressure. The impact is substantial but may be judged more incremental than novel.
uncertainties: The pairing mechanism remains unsettled.
Whether the committee would credit Chen and Zhao for the Tc increase is unclear.
The discovery was partly built on Hosono's earlier oxide pnictide work and the cuprate precedent, which may reduce perceived originality.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Superconductivity in the Bechgaard salts was the first observed in an organic conductor and opened a long line of research in low-dimensional correlated electrons, including spin-density waves, field-induced phases and non-Fermi-liquid behaviour. The discovery is original and conceptually influential.
assessment.attribution: Jérome, Bechgaard and colleagues discovered superconductivity in (TMTSF)2PF6 under pressure in 1980; Bechgaard synthesized the compounds and Jérome led the physics. This two-person allocation seems fair, though Mazaud, Ribault and the broader Orsay group were also involved and Little's earlier theoretical proposal is conceptually relevant.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and independently confirmed over four decades, with stable interpretation as a correlated low-dimensional superconductor. If the prize has not yet been given, recognition is substantially overdue and may look dated, and the pairing symmetry remains debated.
uncertainties: The pairing symmetry and mechanism are still debated.
A late recognition could be judged less timely relative to newer fields.
Contributions of other Orsay and Copenhagen colleagues may complicate a two-person allocation.
